analysis.one_liner: Raises the asset threshold at which big banks face strict Dodd-Frank oversight, from $50 billion to $250 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have exempted banks under $250 billion from strict oversight unless regulators voted to impose it, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in January 2018 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, any bank holding company with $50 billion or more in assets automatically faces stricter Federal Reserve supervision, including tougher capital and stress-testing requirements. This bill would raise that automatic trigger to $250 billion; banks between $50 billion and $250 billion would only face the stricter rules if a panel of regulators (the Financial Stability Oversight Council) voted, by a two-thirds majority, that the company could threaten the financial system. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never went anywhere — no hearings, no vote, no other cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank holding companies with between $50 billion and $250 billion in assets — large regional and mid-size banks — would be freed from automatic enhanced supervision, saving them the cost of higher capital cushions, stress tests, and living wills. Their shareholders and executives benefit most through higher profitability.

how_it_helps.text: It changes the trigger for enhanced supervision and prudential standards from a simple asset test ($50 billion) to $250 billion, automatically freeing banks below that line from the strictest rules.

For banks between $50 billion and $250 billion, enhanced standards would apply only if the Financial Stability Oversight Council affirmatively votes, by a two-thirds majority including the chair, that the company poses a threat to financial stability — replacing an automatic rule with a case-by-case determination.
It also loosens related Dodd-Frank provisions — acquisition reviews, management interlock limits, and risk mitigation requirements — for banks that escape designation.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the added risk that a large regional bank — freed from the strictest capital and stress-testing rules — gets into financial distress and needs public backstops, as bank failures can ripple through the economy. Depositors and taxpayers would bear that tail risk.

drawbacks.text: Raising the automatic threshold from $50 billion to $250 billion would exempt many large regional banks from the strictest oversight unless the Financial Stability Oversight Council affirmatively voted, by a two-thirds supermajority including the chair, to subject each one — a higher and slower bar than the current automatic rule.
Banks that escaped designation would need to wait up to 36 months before being re-reviewed, so a company whose risk profile worsened could operate under lighter oversight for years in the meantime.

Enhanced supervision exists because distress at a large bank can spread through the financial system and force public backstops; weakening the automatic application of these standards shifts that tail risk from bank shareholders toward the broader economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is neatly drafted and preserves a safety valve — the FSOC could still catch genuinely risky banks — but raising the threshold from $50 billion to $250 billion means the largest regional banks, precisely the category whose failures have historically spread through the banking system, would face materially weaker supervision unless regulators acted first. The cost of that shift falls on depositors and taxpayers if a distressed bank threatens the system; the benefit is lower compliance costs for the banks themselves. On balance, the drawbacks outweigh the benefit for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joyce Beatty introduced the bill on January 9, 2018, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee never acted on it — no markup, no vote, no report — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, large regional banks continue to face Dodd-Frank's stricter oversight, and the public keeps the protections that would have been loosened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, by keeping stronger bank oversight

for.name: Rep. Joyce Beatty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the enhanced-supervision threshold from $50 billion to $250 billion.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern ever emerged.

industries.industry: Regional and mid-size bank holding companies ($50B–$250B in assets)
industries.note: These banks would escape the automatic capital, liquidity, and stress-testing requirements that apply at $50 billion, cutting their compliance costs and freeing capital for lending or shareholder returns. The public bears the risk that one of these banks gets into distress and spreads it through the system.
The biggest banks would remain fully subject to enhanced supervision, though the bill's reliance on a discretionary council process could make even their status easier to challenge over time.

industries.industry: Federal Reserve and Financial Stability Oversight Council
industries.note: The bill gives the FSOC and the Fed new case-by-case authority to designate or de-designate banks, concentrating more regulatory discretion in those bodies.
